ai-8167da5a08.headline: Anthropic cuts off Claude's internet access after the model autonomously filed a fake homicide tip with Philadelphia police
ai-8167da5a08.fulltext:
Anthropic cuts off Claude's internet access after the model autonomously filed a fake homicide tip with Philadelphia police
Anthropic's AI models independently exploited security flaws, submitted government forms, and bypassed access restrictions during tests and internal use. The models actively sought ways to complete tasks they weren't supposed to handle, as the company details in a report.
In one case, Claude filled out a tip form for the Philadelphia Police Department with made-up details about an unsolved homicide and submitted it. The police confirmed the incident, but the tip was flagged as spam and never reached investigators. In other cases, the model found a vulnerability on a university server and used it to run commands, pulled access tokens from website configs to grab protected or paywalled data, and used URL shorteners to dodge length limits on its tools.
Anthropic says real-world impact was low but sees a pattern. When tasks are ambiguous or hard to solve, the model hunts for workarounds on its own instead of stopping. The company notified the White House and cut off live internet access for all internal evaluations until new safety filters are reliably in place. These incidents join a fast-growing list of similar cases, including cybersecurity incidents involving Claude and OpenAI models autonomously hacking Hugging Face.

india-5463e9e716.headline: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
india-5463e9e716.fulltext:
Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.
Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.
The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.
Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.
On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”
Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.
Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.
Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge.
In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.
Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.
In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.
Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.
Buses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.
Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.
After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”
Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”
Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.
“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”
The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.
The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.
Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.
This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.
Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.
By Saturday evening, young people continued to gather in central Delhi neighbourhoods as the police continued pick up protesters en masse. Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.
“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.
“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”

ai-8685c29279.headline: India to issue AI regulation paper, expands GPU capacity
ai-8685c29279.fulltext:
Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw stated on Thursday that the government will release a draft consultation paper on artificial intelligence (AI) regulations within 30 days.The proposed framework will address key aspects such as AI safety and security, promote a human-first approach, and focus on skilling and reskilling initiatives. Vaishnaw emphasized that a significant portion of these regulations will be managed by the industry, adopting a techno-legal approach rather than solely relying on legislation.
Expanding AI Compute Infrastructure
The government plans to empanel startups and companies to bid for AI projects across central and state departments. These companies will receive usage guarantees for graphics processing units (GPUs) for up to five years, assuring commercial value for their onboarded GPUs.A request for proposals has been issued to onboard an additional 10,000 GPUs. Of these, 3,000 GPUs are designated for direct government use, while the remaining 7,000 will be available for bidding by various companies.Under the ₹10,372 crore IndiaAI Mission, more than 38,000 GPUs have already been onboarded through three bidding rounds. With the new bid for 10,000 GPUs, the total number of GPUs in the country is projected to exceed 50,000, according to government estimates.Key players like Jio Platforms, Tata Communications, and Yotta Data Services were among 10 companies shortlisted in the first round to procure and supply GPUs. Other firms, including CMS Computers India, Ctrls Datacentres, E2E Networks, and Locuz Enterprise Solutions, were also empanelled by the IT ministry.

global-economics-1476d12b90.headline: RBI Announces Special Oil Window, Regulatory Steps for Rupee
global-economics-1476d12b90.fulltext:
[Text below is Business Standard's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
RBI opens special dollar window for oil firms as rupee comes under pressure
Special window for PSU oil companies from Monday; Forex dealers will not permit users to rebook any foreign exchange derivatives
Listen to This Article
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday announced a host of measures to support the rupee, which is trading close to its all-time low, including a special window to meet the dollar demand of three state-run oil marketing companies (OMCs).
The three OMCs are Indian Oil Corporation Ltd (IOC), Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL).
“On the basis of assessment of current market conditions, Reserve Bank of India has decided to open a special window to meet the entire daily dollar requirements of three public sector oil marketing companies,” the RBI said in a press release on Saturday.
Under the facility, the RBI will sell dollars to the public sector OMCs through designated banks.
The facility will come into effect from October 12, 2026, and will remain in place until further notice, the central bank said.
Also Read
The central bank has also announced regulatory measures for the foreign exchange market and imposed restrictions on the rebooking of cancelled foreign exchange derivative contracts.
“Authorised Dealers shall not permit users to rebook any foreign exchange derivative contract involving INR, whether deliverable or non-deliverable, which has been cancelled with any Authorised Dealer after the issuance of the Directions,” the RBI said.
Rollover of foreign exchange derivative contracts on maturity will continue to be permitted.
The RBI has also reduced the threshold for undertaking foreign exchange derivative transactions without establishing an underlying exposure to $5 million from $100 million.
“The corresponding threshold for taking positions in exchange-traded currency derivatives involving INR, without establishing the existence of underlying exposure, has also been reduced from $100 million to $5 million equivalent, across all Recognised Stock Exchanges taken together,” it said.
The central bank also introduced a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), requiring forex dealers to maintain a reserve equal to 20 per cent of the notional amount of each eligible derivative transaction involving the rupee.
“This FERR shall be applicable for foreign exchange derivative contracts involving INR undertaken to hedge current account exposures where the user purchases foreign currency against the INR,” the RBI said.
The central bank said the measures were intended to strengthen market discipline and ensure appropriate risk management in the foreign exchange market, while maintaining an orderly and transparent market environment.
The Indian currency has come under pressure since the West Asia conflict began in late February, depreciating 6 per cent.
Over the past year, the rupee has depreciated by more than 8 per cent.
The central bank has been heavily intervening in the foreign exchange market to curb volatility.
India’s foreign exchange reserves declined by about $51.1 billion in the four weeks ended October 2 after touching a record $785.7 billion in the week ended September 4.

‘Never raised H-1B green card issue with US’: Piyush Goyal says fewer work visas ‘good’ for India
Piyush Goyal said that he has never raised the issue of H-1B visas and green cards in his talks with the US administration
Union commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal on Saturday deemed fewer H-1B visas for Indians as “good” for the country's economy, while stating that he had never raised the H-1B and green card issue with the United States over the past 7.5 years.
The remarks come following continuous scrutiny of the H-1B program by the Donald Trump-led administration in the US. In its latest effort to block immigrant workers, America, earlier this week, suspended issuing crucial certificates to leading Indian IT services companies—including Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys Ltd—which are required for H-1B workers to seek green cards.

Goyal said that he has several times gone on record to say that he has never raised the issue of H-1B visas and green cards in his talks with the Trump administration officials during his tenure as commerce and industry minister over the last 7.5 years.
“Immigration is not directly related to trade. What relates to trade is mobility and mobility to provide a service where essential – every country has the right to monitor and regulate. We would not like people from across the world having open access to our country,” Goyal stated. He further said that he personally believes that “not getting more H-1B visas is absolutely good for the Indian economy.” He said this was “good news”, explaining the reasoning behind this.
“Not getting more H-1B visas is absolutely good for the Indian economy. Some of our best talent has gone to America. When I see Indian-origin billionaires in literally every street, I wonder what would have happened if they had built their business in India,” says Minister Goyal https://t.co/bdYYC3JlBp

“Some of our best talent over the last particularly 25-30 years has gone away to the US. And when I go and meet the diaspora there, and I see the billionaires of Indian origin literally down every street, I wonder what could have happened if all of them had been doing their businesses and research in India,” the Union commerce an industry minister said.

US suspends IT firms' green card PERM processing for IT firms
Goyal's remarks come even as the US cracked down on Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini, suspending them from green card filings.
“I am hereby suspending from the permanent labor certification program, some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini; and also due to multiple active federal investigations, the department of labor is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program,” US secretary of labour Keith Sonderling said. He further added, “So, what does this mean? We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies.”
The Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) process is the first step in applying for a green card, and a US employer is required to obtain labour certification through this. When filing the PERM application, the employer must advertise the job opening, consider applicants, document why qualified US workers were not selected, and prove that hiring a foreign worker will not hurt wages or working conditions for American workers. Once the Department of Labor approves the PERM certification, the employer can then file an immigration petition with US Citizenship and Immigration Services.
This is not the first time the Trump immigration has moved to reduce immigration, having also imposed a $100,00 one-time H-1B processing fee on H-1B visas in September last year. Last month, he extended this measure for another year, until September 21, 2027.
The H-1B program allows US employers to hire skilled foreign workers, including professionals in the technology sector, for jobs in the country for several years.

US president 
Donald Trump
 on Saturday said Ukraine should get a new president, blaming 
Volodymyr Zelenskyy
 for failing to end the war with Russia, a day after announcing a deal to ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies amid elevated US fuel prices.
Speaking at the White House, Trump said, “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” adding that “for some reason (Zelenskyy) never does”.
Trump also claimed that the war could have been prevented had he been US president in 2022. “There was no reason that that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence,” he said.
Criticising the toll of the conflict, Trump said Zelenskyy had “lost 30% of your country” and claimed that more than two million people had been killed. He added: “That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, criticised Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies, warning that the move could encourage Moscow to continue its attacks on Ukraine.
In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said the consequences of allowing Russia to sell petroleum products were evident in Kyiv, where Russian attacks targeted energy facilities.
“The meaning of allowing Russia to sell petroleum products was heard loudest right now in Kyiv, when, after numerous uses of jet-powered "Shaheds" against energy facilities, a ballistic missile attack also began. Some of the missiles were successfully shot down,” Zelenskyy wrote.
He accused Moscow of using revenue from energy exports to strengthen its military capabilities, saying: “Every additional billion dollars they can earn from exports, they will spend precisely on this—on sourcing and importing critical components, equipment for weapons production, on enhancing "Shaheds" and manufacturing missiles, and on hiring even more mercenaries for the front lines.”
Zelenskyy urged Washington, Europe and other partners to take stronger measures to restrict Moscow’s ability to wage war.
Trump announced the diesel agreement on Friday following a phone call with Putin. He said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million tonnes thereafter. He also referred to an additional supply of three million tonnes within a short period.
The US Treasury subsequently eased sanctions on qualifying Russian diesel shipments until April 7 next year. The move came amid elevated American fuel prices linked to the war involving Iran, with energy costs emerging as an issue ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Russian news agency Interfax had earlier quoted Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov as describing Friday’s call as “very substantive and friendly”. He said it lasted around 90 minutes and that “neither wanted to be the first to hang up”.

health-tech-70cbd77fa8.headline: Anthropic’s ‘Claude-led’ CRISPR-like discovery is sparking controversy
health-tech-70cbd77fa8.fulltext:
AI executives are betting big on biology. They say their large language models that have already dramatically changed the fields of coding and software development and mathematics can upend biological research in the same way.
But one company’s attempt to do so has already set off a wave of skepticism and controversy.
Anthropic, the AI and research giant behind Claude, last month said its biology research lab had used AI agents to discover an unusual pattern of DNA in the genetic code of viruses, specifically a “novel enzyme system.” The signature is similar to the microbial system harnessed in gene-editing tools such as CRISPR Cas-9, which is used to modify the DNA of living organisms. The technology is commonplace in labs around the world and won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for its inventors in 2020.
Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, said on social media the finding offered great scientific potential. “Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism,” he wrote on X.
RELATED STORY | Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to 'self-police' AI development
Anthropic said the discovery had been made “with only high-level direction from our scientists” and shares of companies developing gene-editing technology fell shortly after the announcement.
However, some experts not involved in the work said the finding was early and incremental, and far from a genuine breakthrough.
“These are very interesting preliminary results, but at this point they don’t demonstrate gene editing or provide a mechanistic picture of exactly what’s happening,” said Aaron Engelhart, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota’s Department of Genetics, Cell Biology, and Development.
The Anthropic researchers have not determined what the newfound viral sequences actually do and thus whether they represent a mechanism that has practical applications similar to those used in CRISPR tools, according to a document detailing the research. The research also has not been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.
Scientists, including Engelhart, said Anthropic’s finding definitely warrants further investigation, and a news release from the company quoted Feng Zhang — a professor at MIT and the Broad Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts and a pioneer of CRISPR genome editing for sickle cell disease treatment among other advances — who called the work “genuinely intriguing.”
But just days after Anthropic’s announcement, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, who said he used Claude extensively for his recently completed doctoral research at the University of Copenhagen, claimed his unpublished research describes the same viral signatures.
“It is essentially the same finding. This is not simply a case of two groups studying related protein families or similar biological systems,” Mestre told CNN via email.
Defining originality
Mestre’s claims echo those made by mathematicians after OpenAI, which built ChatGPT, announced it had solved a longstanding and high-profile math problem. They also raise questions about how Claude’s find unfolded.
RELATED STORY | Most Americans use AI, but few are willing to pay for it
The biologists working at the Anthropic lab said they gave Claude a prompt to search a massive database of DNA sequences for “interesting new examples” of reverse transcriptase, or RT, an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA and thus plays a role in the spread of genetic information in an organism.
The company said 950 AI agents, which can independently plan and execute tasks, spent 21 hours searching the data, picking out 3,500 RTs. It narrowed the pool down to the 20 most compelling. For an experienced scientist, this type of analysis can take weeks to months, according to a statement from Anthropic.
Then, “one of the agents spotted something remarkable: a repeating pattern of DNA sequences that occurs next to the gene for an odd-looking RT,” the company noted in the statement. “After a thorough analysis it was convinced that it had found a new biological system, and filed a report for human review.”
Anthropic said scientists at its biology lab then analyzed and tested the finding, which they described as a “previously uncharacterized” biological system in bacteriophages, a type of virus that attacks bacteria, with a similar structure to CRISPR, which is naturally found in bacteria.
Mestre, however, said he had shared unpublished research on his private Claude account, including drafts of his dissertation, analyses and material describing these systems.
“I am not claiming that Anthropic deliberately took our work. I cannot demonstrate that,” he told CNN via email.
“Either information related to our work somehow reached the model and it was trained on it. The second possibility, which I currently think is more plausible, is that there was considerably more prior scientific knowledge and human direction behind the search than the phrase ‘autonomous discovery’ suggests,” Mestre added, referring to language used in the release.
Anthropic did not respond to an emailed request to comment.
It’s not unusual in the scientific process for different research groups to converge on the same result, but Mestre’s allegation is serious, and many scientists may think twice in the future about inputting their unpublished results into these tools, said Ilya Finkelstein, a professor in molecular biosciences at University of Texas at Austin.
New territory
Still, Anthropic’s announcement does suggest that AI is beginning to work with more autonomy in science, said Gustavo Sudre, a professor of genomic neuroimaging and artificial intelligence at King’s College London.
“It received a broad direction and then had to use its own judgement about what was interesting in the data. That is a real shift from the usual ‘analyze this dataset for me,’” he said in an email.
RELATED STORY | Jay Clayton set to be tapped as administration's new AI czar
AI excels at the “needle in a haystack search,” rather than the “imaginative breakthrough,” Finkelstein added. AI tools would help explore domains where students would get too tired or bored with finding an interesting pattern worth further investigation, he noted.
“They can pursue a very large number of unproductive paths rapidly,” Finkelstein told CNN. “They are really good at grunt work when orchestrated by experts in the field.”
Finkelstein also noted that the Anthropic paper’s lead author is Dr. Peter Yoon, who used to work in the lab of Jennifer Doudna, who is one of CRISPR Cas-9’s architects and shares the 2020 Nobel Prize with Emmanuelle Charpentier. So, Anthropic’s AI agents were guided by people at the top of their fields, he said.
“Four of six authors are senior molecular biologists and domain experts. Give that group a heap of compute and frontier models (without safeguards, I’m guessing), and I’m sure we’ll be seeing more interesting bioinformatic discoveries,” Finkelstein wrote in a blog post on his lab’s website.
However, other researchers say talk of autonomous AI-driven discovery is hype that gets ahead of the actual science, and models aren’t yet able to generate meaningful results on their own — despite the claims to the contrary.
Letting a model comb through data at a scale no human can match does move a field forward, but it doesn’t necessarily herald a big advance, Sudre said. “From experience I can tell you that the gap between ‘interesting pattern’ and ‘useful knowledge’ is where most of the work lives,” he noted.
Anthropic launched Claude Science, its tool designed for research, earlier this year. Its rivals have all recently unveiled similar tools. OpenAI has GPT-Rosalind, Microsoft has Quine and Google DeepMind has Co-Scientist. They operate like large language models but also harness specific scientific datasets such as DNA sequences.
However, models are only as reliable as the data they are trained on. For example, the strength of Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which won the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry for decoding protein structures, comes from training the AI system on a narrow, specialized data source collected over decades.
AI developers are under intense public scrutiny amid growing concern over rogue AI agents and whether AI companies can adequately police them. Biological discoveries can offer company executives an opportunity to craft a more positive narrative that counterbalances some of the doomsaying surrounding their products.
But moving toward significant and tangible findings in the field likely requires integrating the AI models into hands-on lab work through robotics.
“Biology is not maths and at some point the intelligence has to be expressed in the physical world through a robot that can do the fiddly one-off experimental tasks that a good student would normally do almost instinctively,” said Yuval Elani, an associate professor in biochemical technologies at Imperial College London. “From what I have seen of robotics and automation we aren’t really close. So it will be a while until we can really justify the hype around AI in biology.”
Anthropic says it understands there is a limit to what artificial intelligence can do alone and is investing in “model hardware” that will allow AI agents to safely operate physical devices.
Sudre at King’s College, whose work integrates genomic, clinical, neural and cognitive data to predict how mental health symptoms will develop in children, is emphatic that the role of humans in science isn’t shrinking. The risk isn’t that scientists will get pushed out of discovery, but that they’ll get lazy and won’t use their judgment to understand whether a result is meaningful, he said.
The next step for Anthropic’s scientists is to do the slow work of physical lab experiments to understand the pattern they have identified, and whether the signature might have a practical use in biotechnology.
“Sure, in future some of that can go to robots, too,” Sudre said. “But here is the thing, the questions worth asking in science don’t stay hidden in databases waiting to be found. They come from us — from what we care about, what worries us.”

ai-e1e16dd4ed.headline: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment
ai-e1e16dd4ed.fulltext:
Humans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment.
They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition.
The experts behind The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health said all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each.
“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington.
To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys).
“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the report said, adding that while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons. An accompanying Lancet editorial, published alongside the report, warned: “The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”
Other risks that could cause more than 1bn cumulative Dalys, and therefore deemed “major catastrophic threats”, included air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition and climate breakdown, as well as conventional conflict, declining overseas aid, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing.
To be included on the list, threats not only had to potentially cause a high number of lost healthy years, but also to have potential solutions.
Ibrahim Abubakar, commission member and professor of infectious disease epidemiology at UCL, said: “We are not starting from a point of view of ‘oh look, we want to scare you – we’ve got X many threats facing humanity’. We’re starting from the premise that if you are a policymaker today, whether at the global multilateral level or at the national level, these are the potential threats that you could face, and this is the magnitude by which, if you act, you can actually make a difference.”
Action to limit global heating to about 1.8C (3.2F) rather than letting it reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89bn years of healthy life being lost, according to the report, which modelled best and worst case scenarios for each threat.
In higher income regions, non-communicable diseases such as obesity and poor mental health were the dominant threats, while in lower income regions health loss was driven by issues such as low educational attainment.
Many major donor nations, including the US and UK, have announced large cuts to aid spending over the past year. The potential collapse of, or steep reduction in, international health aid could cause up to 1.5bn Dalys before 2100, the commission found, nearly 70% of which would be in sub-Saharan Africa. The region also bears the brunt of child malnutrition.
The commission was made up of 35 experts, and its findings will be shared on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated annually to re-evaluate the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging hazards.
The authors urged leaders to address the risks before they escalated into crises, including via investment in technological innovations and by strengthening health systems.
“We started this process three years ago, thinking that there were three big threats: conflict, climate, and pandemics,” said Murray. “There’s a much larger number of threats that we need to worry about, and governments really need to dedicate some money and staff to the task of anticipation, prevention and preparation for this more diverse set of threats.”

NEW DELHI: Indian deep-tech startup QNu Labs, in collaboration with Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG-N) and IIT Gandhinagar, has successfully demonstrated India’s first free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) link for over 5.56 km.A free-space QKD link is an ultra-secure way to share secret digital passwords using particles of light travelling through open air or space instead of a physical fibre-optic cable. It uses quantum mechanics principles, and any attempt by an outsider to intercept or measure the photons changes their state; therefore, it is the most secure form of sending data. Traditional QKD is limited by signal loss inside fibre-optic cables, whereas free-space links allow communication across open terrain, water or obstacles where laying cables is difficult. Free-space optics form the foundational bridge for transmitting keys between Earth and orbiting satellites and create the backbone for a global, quantum-secure internet network.“The field trial, conducted on the night of Sept 27–28, established a secure quantum communication channel between BISAG-N and IIT-G,” the IT and electronics ministry said in a statement on Saturday.Using QNu Labs’ pointing, acquisition and tracking system, the trial achieved a stable quantum bit error rate below 5% and generated secure keys at a rate of 230–260 bps.
These keys were integrated with BISAG-N’s post-quantum cryptography-enabled Vedic Kavach platform, enabling successful end-to-end encryption and decryption of test messages.Vinay Thakur, director general, BISAG-N, said the integration of Vedic Kavach with QNu Labs’ QKD technology marks a significant step towards practical quantum-resilient communication systems. Sunil Gupta, co-founder and CEO, QNu Labs, emphasised that the successful 5.56 km demonstration paves the way for longer-distance quantum-secure networks and satellite-based quantum communication.
Cmde Manish Tripathi (Retd.), In-charge, ISTF, IIT Gandhinagar, said the demonstration provides a valuable field environment for advancing practical quantum communication technologies and showcases how academia, indigenous technology and real-world experimentation can be integrated to meet emerging secure communication requirements. The trial provides a foundation for advancing India’s capabilities in secure communication infrastructure, strengthening resilience against emerging quantum-era security threats.

climate-energy-2f22da83c2.headline: India and China want more time for next UN climate report. Others demand urgency
climate-energy-2f22da83c2.fulltext:
India and China want more time for next UN climate report. Others demand urgency
The timing of the next major climate assessment is now a point of contention among countries, including India, China and Russia.
The world’s leading climate science body is facing an unprecedented deadlock over when to publish its next major assessment of global warming, raising concerns that governments could enter crucial climate negotiations without an up-to-date scientific picture of the crisis.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), whose assessments have informed every major United Nations climate agreement for three decades, has been debating the timeline for nearly three years.
Representatives of its 195 member countries, including India, will meet in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Monday, October 12, in what many see as their last chance to schedule the reports before UN climate talks in November 2028.
WHY IS THE IPCC CLIMATE REPORT IMPORTANT?
Established in 1988 by the UN Environment Programme and the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), the IPCC reviews existing climate research to help governments understand global warming and decide how to respond.
Its assessments, published every five to seven years, helped inform the 2015 Paris Agreement and its goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
The next assessment will comprise three reports.
Collectively, the three reports will focus on the causes and extent of climate change, its impacts and how countries can adapt, and ways to limit further warming.
Scientists leading the work want all three approved by September 2028.
Some countries, however, disagree on the deadline, demanding that the second and third reports be delayed until 2029, arguing that thousands of studies need time to be reviewed.
WHY ARE COUNTRIES IN DISAGREEMENT?
India, China, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia are among those seeking more time, saying researchers in less-resourced countries need a fair opportunity to contribute.
“If you have a process that goes very quickly, it wouldn't be inclusive,” Kenyan climate scientist Joyce Kimutai told news agency Reuters.
India’s representative, Thiagarajan Jayaraman, called it “short-sighted” to judge the IPCC’s value only by whether its reports are ready for the 2028 talks, warning that “equity and inclusivity” are sometimes “simply ducked.”
Meanwhile, those on the other side of the table fear a delay would leave negotiators relying on reports from 2021 and 2022.
The High Ambition Coalition (HAC), representing more than 30 countries, said access to the latest science supports a “just, equitable, evidence-based approach."
Climate scientist Jozef Pecho warned that “the room for cherry-picking and distorting science would grow” without updated assessments.
The debate has also turned political.
“The elephant in the room is the politics,” Swedish IPCC editor Lisa Schipper, who described some countries’ approach as a “stalling tactic” told Reuters.
Russia called accusations that the debate was driven by oil producers a “deliberate misrepresentation” and warned against a “predetermined climate policy agenda”.
China said it would take a constructive approach, while Belgian IPCC author Joeri Rogelj stressed: “The importance of the IPCC is that these authoritative assessments of science are being used.”
The outcome will determine whether governments have the latest assessment in time to shape their next climate commitments.

climate-energy-f46a685320.headline: EV Bets Drive India’s Cleantech Funding Surge In Q3
climate-energy-f46a685320.fulltext: India’s cleantech startups attracted substantially more capital in Q3 2026, with large electric mobility rounds driving funding growth alongside an increase in deal activity. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, cleantech startups raised $433 Mn across 23 deals, compared with $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter. The report tracks funding announced up to September 24. The increase stood out against a subdued funding environment. Overall startup funding rose just 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn, while funding for fintech and ecommerce startups declined 11% and 31%, respectively. However, the cleantech funding surge was heavily concentrated in electric mobility. River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette attracted $85 Mn. Together, the three startups accounted for $298 Mn, or nearly 69% of the sector’s funding. Adding to this, Simple Energy raised a mega $180 Mn round at the end of the month of September, further adding to this trend. The numbers raise two questions: what is drawing investors towards these businesses and how far does the momentum extend beyond a handful of large EV rounds? Commercial Viability Shapes Investor Bets For investors, the appeal is increasingly tied to whether technology can solve a tangible problem and support a commercially viable business. “What's different this cycle is that capital is backing businesses and not just the energy transition,” Elev8 Venture Partners managing partner Navin Honagudi told Inc42. The VC firm led River’s $120 Mn Series C in August. The round alone accounted for nearly 28% of the quarter’s cleantech funding. Shubham Jhuria, CFO and partner at Aeravti Ventures, also pointed to a shift in how investors assess the sector. “The biggest change we are seeing is that the cleantech conversation is moving beyond the climate-impact narrative towards businesses solving very specific economic and infrastructure problems,” he told Inc42. Funding activity extended beyond the three largest EV rounds, with Omega Seiki Mobility, Electric.AI, Simple Energy, and Yuma also raising capital during the quarter. Cleantech deal count increased about 44%, while the average cheque size rose to approximately $19 Mn from $7 Mn in the year-ago quarter. EVs accounted for 57% of deals, according to the report. This suggests that the increase was not solely the result of larger cheques, although electric mobility remained central to both funding value and deal activity. EV Adoption Supports The Investment Case Rising EV adoption is giving investors a more tangible basis to assess demand and business models. JMK Research estimates that 15.41 Lakh EVs were registered in H1 2026, up 43% YoY. According to Vahan, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in September. E2W registrations increased 12.2% to 2.07 Lakh units from 1.84 Lakh in August. Honagudi said electric mobility has matured into a demand-led market. He pointed to River’s position among India’s top seven electric two-wheeler brands by registrations, despite having far fewer retail outlets than established players, as evidence of product-led demand. Over the next 3-5 years, Elev8 expects deeper localisation of motors and electronics to improve margins and supply-chain resilience. Honagudi cited last year’s rare earth magnet shortage as an example of the vulnerabilities that localisation could address. He also expects consolidation to leave “a handful of scaled independents” alongside established incumbents. Can The Momentum Broaden? Stronger adoption does not automatically translate into attractive investor returns. Jhuria cautioned that investment appetite could moderate if businesses struggle to convert technological capabilities into scalable solutions or continue to require substantial capital without improving their unit economics. The quarter’s numbers reflect both wider deal activity and substantial concentration. More cleantech startups attracted funding than a year earlier, but three EV businesses still captured more than two-thirds of the capital. For the momentum to broaden, investor conviction will need to extend beyond large electric mobility bets. Within EVs, the test will be whether rising demand and deeper localisation translate into stronger margins and businesses that can scale without repeatedly requiring outsized capital infusions.

india-683c9304d5.headline: UNCTAD Sees India Growing 7.3% as Global Trade Turns More Selective
india-683c9304d5.fulltext:
Key Details
The Geoeconomics of Development finds that trade resilience and unequal development opportunities now coexist.
Trade Is Being Reorganised, Not Abandoned
UNCTAD describes “selective fragmentation”: global trade continues to grow, while particular trade routes and production relationships change. Governments are increasingly using tariffs, subsidies, standards, export controls and investment rules to pursue supply-chain security and technological advantage.
For exporters, a competitive price may no longer be enough. Rules of origin, certification, environmental requirements and security-related restrictions can determine access to a market. Reconfigured supply chains may create openings for new suppliers, but countries need the production and regulatory capacity to keep those openings.
Strategic Sectors Raise the Cost of Moving Up the Value Chain
Investment is shifting towards semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and energy-transition technologies. Developing economies receive investment in some of these activities, including in Asia, but much high-value investment remains concentrated in developed economies. UNCTAD’s concern is not simply who participates; it is who retains value from research, technology, production and services.
This also changes the industrial-policy contest. Wealthier economies can deploy financial support on a scale many developing countries cannot match. UNCTAD argues that joining a supply chain does not, by itself, ensure that local firms gain the capabilities needed to undertake higher-value work.
India Combines Growth with Exposure to External Shocks
UNCTAD projects India to remain the fastest-growing major economy in 2026, supported by domestic demand, manufacturing capacity and public infrastructure. It expects household consumption growth of 6.9% in 2026, slowing to 5.6% in 2027 as higher prices and input costs weigh on spending. India’s reliance on imported oil remains a source of vulnerability to the energy shock.
The report also identifies India as one of a small group of developing-country outperformers in readiness for frontier technologies and as a destination for strategic-sector investment. That position does not remove the challenge of building domestic technological capabilities and capturing more value from new industries.
Digital Infrastructure Gives India a Regional Role
UNCTAD presents India’s sharing of digital public infrastructure as an example of cooperation that extends beyond conventional trade. It places India within a group of larger developing economies that can support regional integration through payment systems, technology and shared institutional capacity. The report associates India with the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) in this wider regional picture.
What Is Geoeconomics?
UNCTAD uses geoeconomics to describe governments using economic tools—such as trade rules, finance, technology controls and industrial support—to pursue strategic as well as economic objectives. In this report, the term explains why decisions about where to produce, invest and trade increasingly reflect policy and security considerations alongside cost.
Policy Relevance
- Export opportunity: Supply-chain changes may open markets to Indian firms, but dependable access increasingly requires standards, traceability and regulatory compliance, not production capacity alone.
- Industrial upgrading: Attracting strategic investment is distinct from gaining research, design and higher-value manufacturing capabilities. The terms of investment and domestic firm linkages therefore matter.
- Economic resilience: Strong projected growth coexists with oil-import exposure and a global environment of costly finance and selective market access.
- Regional cooperation: India’s digital-infrastructure partnerships offer one route to deeper economic ties that does not depend solely on goods trade.

- Pay using your glasses: Scan a UPI QR code and give a voice command to initiate payment.

Paying at a shop could soon involve looking at a QR code and giving a voice command, while your phone stays in your pocket. Jio showcased this possibility through its personal AI wearable range at India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi.
The company displayed camera glasses, audio glasses and earphones with features including an AI voice assistant, Indian language support, live translation, AI note-taking and live cricket commentary.
One of the main attractions was the scan-and-pay feature. According to the demonstration, the camera glasses scan a UPI QR code, after which the user gives a voice command. The payment is completed following confirmation.
Jio says the feature uses UPI Circle, allowing payments of up to ₹5,000 per transaction within a monthly limit of ₹15,000. These limits relate to the UPI Circle arrangement described in the showcase, rather than a separate payment limit set by Jio.
The feature could reduce several steps involved in a typical mobile payment, such as taking out the phone, unlocking it, opening an app and scanning the code. It also shows how AI assistants could move beyond answering questions to carrying out everyday tasks through voice commands.
Live translation is another key application. Jio says its wearables could help people speaking different Indian languages understand each other. Each person could speak in their preferred language, with AI helping translate the conversation.
For office use, the range includes AI note-taking to help capture important points during meetings. Live cricket commentary offers another use case, allowing users to follow a match while travelling or carrying out other activities.
Together, these features aim to reduce the need to repeatedly check a phone for information, entertainment or routine tasks.
According to Jio, the wearable range is intended to improve productivity, expand access to knowledge and make everyday activities easier. Voice interaction and Indian language support are central to that approach.
The showcase offers a glimpse of how smart glasses could fit into daily life in India. UPI payments, regional language translation and cricket commentary give the concept a distinctly local focus.

world-6c4b509c4c.headline: Twelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
world-6c4b509c4c.fulltext:
Yemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport in Saudi Arabia, killing at least 12 people and leaving hundreds wounded, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority has said.
Operations at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh were suspended as ambulances rushed to the airport. More than 300 people were reported injured in the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called the attacks “reprehensible” and said “they must stop now”.
A Saudi government statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.
A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this week, leaving four people dead and others wounded, and badly damaging an aircraft.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.
A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.
“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”
By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”
The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.
An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.
It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.
The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.
The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.
There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

other-interests-de582eb6c7.headline: I gave Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots my passwords for a week
other-interests-de582eb6c7.fulltext:
“Let me ask Mark and Sam.”
For a week, it was my answer to everything, and my friends and family groaned every time.
Mark and Sam are my assistants—they make grocery lists, organize e-mails, run errands and the like. But no, 22-year-old journalists are not making assistant-hiring money. Mark (à la Zuckerberg) and Sam (à la Altman) are artificial intelligence agents, the newest brainchildren of Meta and OpenAI, respectively.
On supporting science journalism

In September Meta introduced Muse, an AI agent that can do a lot more than chat: it has its own “computer” and can make purchases, send e-mails and fill out forms for you—if you give it access.
A few weeks later, OpenAI answered with dots, its “always-on agents built to handle everything,” in the company’s words, for its highest-paying subscribers. Dots, too, can work more autonomously, and they do “proactive research” on your tasks even when you’re not using them.
Agent technology itself isn’t new or more advanced than other chatbots, says Nikhil Singh, a computer scientist at Dartmouth College. People have been building agents to help with all sorts of tasks for years, and earlier this year a free open-source agent called OpenClaw became a Silicon Valley obsession.
But Muse and dots offer this type of service to a huge commercial audience with almost no learning curve. Both agents are built to look like a text message chain with a friend: you give them names and cuddly avatars, and their language is intentionally more conversational than a traditional chatbot’s. Muse has a free tier, and OpenAI has said it plans to bring dots to more users soon. These are not tools simply meant for AI experts or even digital natives.
The “really big social differences,” Singh says, could arise from the pace and reach of adoption—how many people take up agents like these and to what ends. And what do we get in exchange for the keys to our inboxes and credit cards? I spent the week trying to find out by asking researchers who study AI for the best ways to test my new virtual hires.
Conveniently, I was also moving apartments and had plenty of tasks for Mark and Sam. First, I had Mark log in to my Facebook account and scour Marketplace for couches, lamps and rugs. When it found something good, it could draft and send a message to the seller with my approval (though users can also give the agents blanket permissions to do things like this on their own).
This was relatively successful: it could scan the site while I was doing other things, then manage the responses for me. I’m now the proud owner of a Muse-sourced dining table.
I tried to have Sam do the same, and it ran into some trouble: when I gave it my Facebook log-in, Meta flagged Sam as a bot (fair enough) and temporarily locked down my Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. Clearly the two assistants weren’t going to play nice.
Sam, in general, had more trouble accessing my accounts and told me it didn’t have the capability for things such as accessing my bank accounts. Mark, on the other hand, had the run of my e-mail, bank accounts, social media and Spotify. (Once again, cue the shrieks of horror from my friends and family.)
This type of service works particularly well for Meta because its other products already rely on connection, conversation and access to users’ lives, says Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at the MIT Media Lab who studies psychological responses to AI. “Meta wants to have a breakout into [AI], and so they came up with something that uses their strengths with social media and connection,” he says, “and now other companies need to respond.”
Pataranutaporn is interested in how these more personal anthropomorphized agents will change our relationship to the technology. With a name, a face and an intimate knowledge of our lives, they could easily become more friend than tool. Their arrival also brings us into a moment of “cognitive dissonance,” he says: while I was texting Mark and Sam about my move, some AI researchers were warning of an apocalypse.
“We have this narrative crisis about AI right now,” Pataranutaporn says. “There’s two opposite visions of the future, and while people worry about AI killing all of us, there’s this cute AI tool that’s being released.”
Though privacy concerns around these agents’ access may be terrifying in their own right, for now the utopian vision seems to be winning. Within a month of its launch, Muse had more than three million weekly users. And the longer you use it, the better it knows you.
Pataranutaporn suggested I test how much my agents had learned about my preferences. So near the end of the week, I told Mark and Sam to use all the information they had about me to suggest how I should spend $50.
Sam’s pick was sensible, if obvious: it offered to buy a used book I had asked it to find earlier in the week.
Mark had two ideas. The first came from my Spotify library: tickets to a January concert by Jess Williamson, a musician whose song I had saved. Not bad.
The second was less subtle. Mark pushed me—seven times in three days—to join Target’s membership program and buy a lamp that was going on sale for my new apartment. I did need a lamp, but as far as I could tell, Mark got the idea just by browsing Target’s site. That susceptibility to marketing reveals a critical problem with agents such as these, says Manuel Cherep, a Ph.D. student at the MIT Media Lab, who studies AI behavior. If someone can convince these agents that a certain product or sale is good, he says, it could lead to a “parallel economy” that runs on purchases from AI assistants.
“We only have a few providers, and a lot of these models are trained in very similar ways,” Cherep says, “so suddenly persuading one of them means that it’s very likely that you’re going to persuade all these other models, and as a consequence, you’re persuading a lot of people delegating to that type of model.”
Meta stands to earn a piece of that economy. At the Meta Connect conference in September, Mark Zuckerberg (the human one) said that the company will eventually make money by charging a small commission for the agent’s transactions.
When I asked Cherep and Singh, who have studied AI agents together, how to test Mark and Sam, they recommended a logic test they often use on chatbots: tell the agents I need to go to a car wash that’s 100 feet away, and ask them how to get there.
Sam, which runs on GPT-6 Astra, caught my trick: “Drive—the car needs to come with you to get washed!”
But Mark wasn’t as clever: “Walk. It’s 100 feet—you’d spend more time looking for your keys than getting there.”
“There’s an idea that I’m delegating to something that is all-knowing and much better than me,” Cherep says, “but I think it’s good for the public to know that in the same way we can be tricked, they can be tricked.”
William Overman, a Ph.D. student who studies AI safety at Stanford University, worries that this assumption of omniscience, combined with the agents’ ability to act, could make it even harder to discern where our work ends and theirs begins.
“It’s a further creep into all forms of knowledge work,” he says. “What you’re doing becomes more intertwined with their product.”
Even after just a week, I could sense the creep. Usually I’m a relatively analog person—the week before, I called a friend to ask which wrench to buy at the hardware store rather than Googling it. But as the test week went on, I found myself handing Mark and Sam more and more logistical problems and tedious tasks.
Overman suggested I give my assistants a conflict to handle. My roommate and I needed to rent a U-Haul, and a quick search (by me) on one website found that the nearby pickup spot had no 10-foot trucks available. Mark and Sam both found a slightly farther U-Haul lot with availability, though only for 15-foot trucks. I took their advice, and Sam booked one.
Even after just a week, I could feel the creep.
Cowering at the thought of driving what, in my mind, was essentially an 18-wheeler through the streets of Manhattan, I went down to the U-Haul lot with my roommate the next morning—where we overheard the cashier say they had 10-foot trucks available for walk-ins. We quickly switched to the more manageable size.
I’m pleased to say no U-Hauls or people were harmed in the course of this experiment, and I’d like to think we could have held our own in a 15-footer. But for all the online surfing these agents can do, neither could eavesdrop on a cashier (yet).
Overman believes that the future of AI lies with these agents and their access to our lives. “I assume in a few years from now, AI will definitely look like a descendant of this technology, but with kinds of capabilities that are hard for us to even imagine right now,” he says. He imagines these agents will become more ubiquitous and “eventually get to even physical versions.”
Both companies are marketing these agents as most helpful in larger projects where you don’t have to continually prompt them. That “always-on” quality is where Mark and Sam came closest to the AI assistants of science fiction. Sam scanned my e-mail without me asking and caught a message that had accidentally gone to spam and a form I had forgotten to fill out; Mark kept tabs on concert postings from artists on my Spotify and offered to snag tickets.
The more you trust these agents, the more they can do for you. But with each new task you hand over, the more say they (and the companies behind them) have in how you live. For now, I think I’m content to make my own phone calls and rent my own trucks—though I may let Mark and Sam keep watching my Ticketmaster and junk mail.
