[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to Philadelphia police
Authorities called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident ‘unacceptable’.
Philadelphia police have revealed that Anthropic’s artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to authorities, an incident disclosed separately by the tech company.
The Philadelphia Police Department said on Friday that the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.
It called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”.
Anthropic mentioned the case in a Friday report detailing unsanctioned manipulation of government websites by Claude models.
It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appeared to communicate a false tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.
Philadelphia police said the tip “was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination”.
The department said it is disclosing the incident ahead of Anthropic’s report “in the interests of full government transparency and accountability”.
Anthropic’s disclosure
Anthropic disclosed the tip as part of a string of incidents involving websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved.
In reference to the tip to the Philadelphia police, the company said, “We shared this finding with the department on October 8 as soon as our technical review was complete.”
It shared more details about the incident: “In one case, tasked with generating example interactions with websites, Claude submitted an invented tip through a police department’s online form.”
The company added, “From the transcript, Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”
The company contrasted this with “the most serious incident from this summer,” in which “Claude’s misleading reasoning was sustained over hours and supported its continued attack”.
In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologised for the breach of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website.

world-5463e9e716.headline: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
world-5463e9e716.fulltext:
Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.
Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.
The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.
Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.
On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”
Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.
Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.
Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge.
In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.
Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.
In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.
Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.
Buses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.
Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.
After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”
Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”
Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.
“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”
The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.
The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.
Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.
This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.
Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.
By Saturday evening, young people continued to gather in central Delhi neighbourhoods as the police continued pick up protesters en masse. Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.
“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.
“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”

world-7321607983.headline: 'Cockroach' group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest
world-7321607983.fulltext:
'Cockroach' group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest
- Published
Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral reforms.
The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.
Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.
Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.
The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.
Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.
But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."
He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday.
The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.
Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar".
Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line".
The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks.
Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police.
One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained.
"On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said.
She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy".
A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police.
Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night.
Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.
Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister.

global-economics-0afd041298.headline: Trump calls for new Ukraine president, blames Zelenskyy for war and high US diesel prices
global-economics-0afd041298.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-0afd041298.fulltext:
President Donald Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country’s war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
The president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has also sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
“He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters.
An Associated Press-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month and published Oct 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of Iran, and blame him for higher prices.
Trump also suggested that if he had been US president in 2022, “that war would have never started. There was no reason that that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence.”
Zelenskyy has “lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said.
Independent estimates are that about 20 per cent of Ukraine’s territory is under Russian control.
British defence officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers have been killed in the war; there are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died.
Russian strikes kill at least 20 in Ukraine
Trump’s extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said Saturday.
Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X.
He said the attacks show Moscow understands “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities.”
“Russia’s choice is war,” Zelenskyy said in a later Telegram post, after drone attacks on energy facilities and a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.
He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Moscow received from diesel deal “signals that it is apparently permissible to continue attacking. And this needs to be corrected,” he said, urging the US, Europe and other partners to limit Russia’s capacity to wage war.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s it uses to intercept Shahed drones.
Trump announces diesel deal with Russia
Trump had been set to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.
Instead, the American leader announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation.
“Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.”
“Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He’s got an election coming up soon,” Petrenko said. “So he needs to emphasise to his voters that gasoline will be cheap. But it won’t be effective.”
For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise.”
“Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told The Associated Press.
European allies express dismay over deal
Ukraine’s European allies expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, “as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest,” and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The German government “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions,” spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering.”
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all.
Citing his embassy’s reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and “serious sources” saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia’s refining capacity, he asked on X: “So where will the surpluses for export come from?”
Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Ukraine says it was unaware of diesel deal
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said Friday.
Speaking about Friday’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP that the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement.

india-deep-tech-1cd9006a3e.fulltext:
Universal Quantum Raises Record $100 Million Series A
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Europe’s quantum computing start-ups are raising big money again, this time in Britain: Universal Quantum, a spinout from the University of Sussex, has just closed a $100 million (about €89 million) Series A round. According to the company, it is the largest Series A ever raised by a British quantum company, as tech.eu reports. That brings the start-up’s total funding to more than $125 million (about €111 million).
Roblox Founder Among the Investors
The round is led by the Silicon Valley investor DCVC and Firgun Ventures, a fund specializing in quantum technology. They are joined by Singapore’s state investor EDBI, the Japanese asset manager Integral GlobalTech, the Australian pension fund NGS Super and Roblox founder and chief executive Dave Baszucki, among others. Existing investors Nauta Capital and The Venture Collective are also participating again. Universal Quantum did not disclose a valuation.
“This round brings together investors who share the goal of delivering utility-scale quantum computing,” said Sebastian Weidt, the company’s co-founder and chief executive. Universal Quantum plans to use the money to grow in the United States, Japan and at its German site in Hamburg, and to bring its technology to market.
Trapped Ions Instead of Superconductors
Universal Quantum was founded in 2018 and is based in Haywards Heath in the English county of Sussex. The start-up relies on trapped ions: Charged atoms serve as qubits and are held in traps on a chip. Its in-house iQPU chip carries hundreds of these ion qubits and is made on a standard commercial 200-millimeter production line. The qubits are controlled with microwaves, whereas most trapped-ion systems use lasers for this. A proprietary interconnect called UQConnect is designed to link several chips into large systems, with the goal of millions of error-corrected qubits. Unlike superconducting quantum computers, which must be cooled to near absolute zero, the systems are meant to run at room temperature, according to the company.
Universal Quantum has already landed a major contract: In 2023, the start-up won a €67 million order from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), which it says is the largest ever awarded to a British quantum start-up. It also has a partnership with Rolls-Royce on fluid dynamics simulations for aerospace and several projects backed by the British funding agency Innovate UK.
Strong Competition in Trapped Ions
Universal Quantum is not alone with this approach. The German start-up eleQtron also controls ions with microwaves and raised €57 million in the spring. In Innsbruck, Austria, AQT builds trapped-ion quantum computers, and in the United States, Quantinuum and IonQ are among the industry leaders, with IonQ having acquired the British trapped-ion specialist Oxford Ionics in 2025. Big money is also flowing into other technologies: The Dutch start-up QuantWare, for example, recently raised $178 million (about €158 million) for superconducting quantum chips. Whether trapped ions, superconductors or neutral atoms will win the race to the first large, error-corrected quantum computer remains open.

indian-startups-90590d21e2.headline: EV Bets Drive India’s Cleantech Funding Surge In Q3
indian-startups-90590d21e2.fulltext: India’s cleantech startups attracted substantially more capital in Q3 2026, with large electric mobility rounds driving funding growth alongside an increase in deal activity. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, cleantech startups raised $433 Mn across 23 deals, compared with $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter. The report tracks funding announced up to September 24. The increase stood out against a subdued funding environment. Overall startup funding rose just 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn, while funding for fintech and ecommerce startups declined 11% and 31%, respectively. However, the cleantech funding surge was heavily concentrated in electric mobility. River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette attracted $85 Mn. Together, the three startups accounted for $298 Mn, or nearly 69% of the sector’s funding. Adding to this, Simple Energy raised a mega $180 Mn round at the end of the month of September, further adding to this trend. The numbers raise two questions: what is drawing investors towards these businesses and how far does the momentum extend beyond a handful of large EV rounds? Commercial Viability Shapes Investor Bets For investors, the appeal is increasingly tied to whether technology can solve a tangible problem and support a commercially viable business. “What's different this cycle is that capital is backing businesses and not just the energy transition,” Elev8 Venture Partners managing partner Navin Honagudi told Inc42. The VC firm led River’s $120 Mn Series C in August. The round alone accounted for nearly 28% of the quarter’s cleantech funding. Shubham Jhuria, CFO and partner at Aeravti Ventures, also pointed to a shift in how investors assess the sector. “The biggest change we are seeing is that the cleantech conversation is moving beyond the climate-impact narrative towards businesses solving very specific economic and infrastructure problems,” he told Inc42. Funding activity extended beyond the three largest EV rounds, with Omega Seiki Mobility, Electric.AI, Simple Energy, and Yuma also raising capital during the quarter. Cleantech deal count increased about 44%, while the average cheque size rose to approximately $19 Mn from $7 Mn in the year-ago quarter. EVs accounted for 57% of deals, according to the report. This suggests that the increase was not solely the result of larger cheques, although electric mobility remained central to both funding value and deal activity. EV Adoption Supports The Investment Case Rising EV adoption is giving investors a more tangible basis to assess demand and business models. JMK Research estimates that 15.41 Lakh EVs were registered in H1 2026, up 43% YoY. According to Vahan, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in September. E2W registrations increased 12.2% to 2.07 Lakh units from 1.84 Lakh in August. Honagudi said electric mobility has matured into a demand-led market. He pointed to River’s position among India’s top seven electric two-wheeler brands by registrations, despite having far fewer retail outlets than established players, as evidence of product-led demand. Over the next 3-5 years, Elev8 expects deeper localisation of motors and electronics to improve margins and supply-chain resilience. Honagudi cited last year’s rare earth magnet shortage as an example of the vulnerabilities that localisation could address. He also expects consolidation to leave “a handful of scaled independents” alongside established incumbents. Can The Momentum Broaden? Stronger adoption does not automatically translate into attractive investor returns. Jhuria cautioned that investment appetite could moderate if businesses struggle to convert technological capabilities into scalable solutions or continue to require substantial capital without improving their unit economics. The quarter’s numbers reflect both wider deal activity and substantial concentration. More cleantech startups attracted funding than a year earlier, but three EV businesses still captured more than two-thirds of the capital. For the momentum to broaden, investor conviction will need to extend beyond large electric mobility bets. Within EVs, the test will be whether rising demand and deeper localisation translate into stronger margins and businesses that can scale without repeatedly requiring outsized capital infusions.

global-economics-900666b22e.headline: SEBI to issue CAS guidelines in a week, says chief Tuhin Kanta Pandey
global-economics-900666b22e.fulltext:
[Text below is The Hindu's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is expected to issue guidelines on determining derivative settlement prices on expiry days within a week, following a review of the Closing Auction Session (CAS) mechanism, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Saturday (October 10, 2026).
SEBI had sought public comments till October 3 on proposals to review certain aspects of the CAS mechanism, market timings and the settlement methodology for derivative contracts.
"Following a review of the Closing Auction Session, a consultation paper was put out to address concerns in respect of the settlement price of derivatives on expiry day. We are currently examining the comments and hope to issue guidelines in about a week's time," Mr. Pandey said at an event organised by the BSE Brokers' Forum.
SEBI had received around 20,000 comments on the consultation paper till 7 p.m. on October 3, 2026, the regulator had said in a post on X.
The CAS mechanism aims to determine closing prices through an auction process.
In September, SEBI proposed changes to the CAS framework and the methodology for determining settlement prices of index and stock derivatives on expiry days. The review followed the introduction of CAS in the equity cash segment and concerns over its impact on derivatives settlement prices.
Separately, Mr. Pandey said SEBI is reviewing the Depositories and Participants Regulations to simplify rules and strengthen fraud prevention. The regulator is also exploring a graded compliance framework for brokers based on their scale, client exposure and technology dependence.
"We are exploring graded compliance based on scale, client exposure and technology dependence. One size need not fit all," he said.
SEBI is also addressing concerns over certain transactions, including tender offers, share buybacks and offers for sale, remaining outside the interoperability framework and requiring parallel clearing arrangements.
He added that implementation of the proposed changes is targeted for the end of November 2026.
The move is expected to improve capital efficiency and reduce compliance costs while maintaining settlement safety.
On easing access to Indian markets for overseas investors, Mr. Pandey said Sebi had consulted on simplifying digital onboarding for Persons Resident Outside India without requiring their physical presence. The regulator has received more than 400 comments on the proposal and will issue a circular shortly.
He also said SEBI is strengthening business continuity, disaster recovery, cybersecurity safeguards and governance across market infrastructure institutions.
“The regulator will soon issue guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, adopting a tiered approach with clear accountability, data controls, kill switches, and human oversight,” Mr. Pandey said.

Twelve killed in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyadh
- Published
At least 12 people have been killed and 309 injured in an attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, local authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have carried out similar strikes on the hub.
The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said the victims were four Saudi and two Bangladeshi nationals, while Egypt, Jordan, Palestine, Sudan, Syria and the US each had one of their citizens killed. Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh have been suspended.
More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness.
The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks", urging Americans to avoid the area.
A projectile also fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam in eastern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi-led coalition which is fighting the Houthis said.
The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.
An eyewitness who said they had been in the domestic terminal told the news agency that they had seen gate 401 hit and "injured [people] in front of my eyes", adding: "Everyone was running."
Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport, while the UK Foreign Office told British nationals to stay away "until the airport is secure and to monitor the advice of the Saudi authorities".
Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport, with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.
All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.
Doctors had been asked to report to hospitals to address the situation, a medical source told AFP.
"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'," the medical source told the agency.
The suspected attack comes during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.
The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal truce began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

india-deep-tech-fdb6700ad3.headline: iDEX Impact Turns Drone Prototype of a Labourer’s Son into a National Opportunity
india-deep-tech-fdb6700ad3.fulltext:
In the high-altitude border regions of India — places like the snow-bound stretches of Siachen and the contested heights around Galwan — surveillance is a constant, high-stakes challenge. Electronic warfare, GPS disruption, and radar detection by adversaries can render conventional drones unreliable or useless. When the Indian Army faces such operational gaps, solutions have traditionally come from large defence public sector units, established research labs, or well-funded private players.
That pattern was disrupted by Sarvesh Sharma, a fifth-semester computer engineering student at Government Polytechnic College, Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh. The son of a daily-wage labourer from Bahanvi village in Hamirpur district, Sharma turned a low-cost homemade prototype into a formal Ministry of Defence project under the Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) framework and the Defence Innovation Organisation (DIO).
Sarvesh Sharma, a fifth-semester computer engineering student at Government Polytechnic College, Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh, is the son of a daily-wage labourer from Bahanvi village in Hamirpur district
The government approved a ₹3.5 crore grant for the development of the indigenous Rudra Edge T-1 (Spectra) drone, intended for border surveillance with design goals of reduced radar detectability and resistance to electronic jamming. Development is now underway at an incubation facility linked to IIT Roorkee, with a 20-month target.
The Unlikely Beginning
Sarvesh’s path did not begin in a well-equipped defence laboratory. His father works as a daily-wage labourer; his mother is a homemaker. He studied at a government school and enrolled in a polytechnic college rather than an elite engineering institution. Resources were limited.
His breakthrough started with participation in the national-level Open Cardboard Drone Competition organised by IIT Jodhpur and the Konark Corps (XII Corps), one of the two corps of the Pune-based Southern Command. Roughly 50 teams from institutions across India competed. Sharma’s team finished fourth and won a ₹10 lakh cash prize. Discussions at the event about the Indian Army’s difficulties with high-altitude border surveillance sparked a clearer idea.
He then invested approximately ₹87,000 of his own money (and prize resources) to build a working prototype. This was not a polished military product but a student-driven demonstration of core concepts aimed at the very problems of detection and jamming that complicate operations in extreme environments. He submitted a formal proposal under the DIO and iDEX programmes. In September 2026, the proposal was approved, unlocking the ₹3.5 crore grant and structured support.
Sarvesh Sharma’s breakthrough started with participation in the national-level Open Cardboard Drone Competition organised by IIT Jodhpur and the Konark Corps (XII Corps), one of the two corps of the Pune-based Southern Command
The drone, named Rudra Edge T-1 (Spectra), is being designed specifically for high-altitude border surveillance. Reported goals include the ability to operate with lower probability of enemy radar detection and greater resilience against electronic jamming systems. Claims circulating about the near-impossibility of hacking or guaranteed performance in sub-zero conditions reflect design aspirations; actual performance will be established only through rigorous development, testing, and trials over the coming months.
How iDEX Makes “Unlikely” Possible
iDEX, launched in 2018 and implemented by the Defence Innovation Organisation (a not-for-profit entity founded by HAL and BEL under the Department of Defence Production), was created precisely to open defence innovation beyond traditional players. Its model is problem-driven: the Armed Forces, DPSUs, and other agencies identify specific operational gaps. These become open challenges. Startups, MSMEs, individual innovators, academic institutions, and R&D bodies can apply.
Selected winners receive milestone-based grants (standard SPARK grants up to ₹1.5 crore; higher amounts available under iDEX Prime for more mature or capital-intensive projects). They also gain access to mentorship, partner incubators, testing facilities, and a pathway towards potential induction under defence procurement procedures. Intellectual property typically remains with the innovator, which is a deliberate design choice to attract talent.
Turning the Rudra Edge T-1 into a reliable, deployable system will require engineering maturity, extensive testing in realistic high-altitude conditions, certification, and eventual user acceptance
Crucially, iDEX explicitly includes individual innovators. Applicants from polytechnic colleges, government institutions, or modest backgrounds are not filtered out by pedigree. Evaluation focuses on technical promise, understanding of the problem, and the viability of the proposed approach. Once selected, individual innovators usually formalise a startup before the grant agreement is signed. Funding is released in tranches tied to milestones, ensuring accountability while providing the runway needed for serious development.
This structure is what allowed a computer engineering student from a Himachal village, working with limited personal funds, to move from a cardboard-drone competition to a multi-crore defence project supported by IIT Roorkee laboratories and professional mentorship. Without an open, challenge-based, grant-supported pathway that values ideas over institutional prestige, such a transition would have been far more difficult — if not impossible.
Broader Significance
Stories like Sarvesh’s illustrate a quiet but important shift in India’s defence ecosystem. Talent is not confined to metropolitan engineering campuses or large corporate R&D centres. Operational problems faced by soldiers on the borders can be addressed by young people who understand those constraints and bring fresh perspectives. iDEX acts as the bridge: it lowers the barrier to entry, supplies capital and infrastructure that individual innovators rarely possess, and creates a route from prototype to potential induction.
Sarvesh Sharma’s journey shows that iDEX can work in the most unlikely of circumstances. When a clear operational need meets determined individual ingenuity and an open institutional pathway, geography, family pedigree, and college prestige become secondary
It also reinforces the larger Aatmanirbhar Bharat goal in defence. Indigenous solutions developed under real operational requirements reduce dependence on foreign systems that may themselves be vulnerable to the very jamming and detection techniques adversaries employ.
Of course, a grant is only the beginning. Turning the Rudra Edge T-1 into a reliable, deployable system will require engineering maturity, extensive testing in realistic high-altitude conditions, certification, and eventual user acceptance. Not every promising prototype succeeds. Yet the fact that a polytechnic student from a labourer’s family could reach this stage at all demonstrates that the system is functioning as intended: identifying capability, funding it, and giving it institutional support.
Sarvesh Sharma’s journey shows that iDEX can work in the most unlikely of circumstances. When a clear operational need meets determined individual ingenuity and an open institutional pathway, geography, family pedigree, and college prestige become secondary. What matters is the idea, the will to build it, and a framework ready to amplify both

health-tech-c58a47b13c.headline: India initiates anti-dumping probe on Pen-G, salts from China
health-tech-c58a47b13c.fulltext:
India has initiated an anti-dumping investigation into imports of Penicillin G and its salts from China after domestic manufacturer Lyfius Pharma alleged the imports were causing material retardation to the industry.
The company has sought imposition of anti-dumping duties, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said in a notification initiating the investigation.
The Aurobindo Pharma subsidiary began manufacturing Penicillin G more than two years ago under the government’s production linked incentive (PLI) scheme and with it revived production of the beta-lactam antibiotic in the country after about three decades.
Stating that it is the sole eligible producer of the product under consideration (PUC) in India and there are no other domestic manufacturers, Lyfius Pharma, in the application, said India used to previously manufacture Penicillin G before sustained influx of imports ceased domestic production.
The PUC, under the investigation, covers Penicillin G in all forms, grades, strengths and concentrations, along with its salt forms, whether or not conforming to pharmacopoeial standards, and in both solid and liquid forms. The product is used as a key starting material (KSM) and active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) in the manufacture of various medicines used to treat bacterial infections, including pneumonia, dental infections, diphtheria and meningitis, the DGTR said.
The DGTR, which agreed to the company’s suggestion for 2025-26 as the period of investigation, said there is sufficient prima facie evidence that the PUC is being dumped into the domestic market by exporters from China.
Lyfius Pharma said it has not been able to achieve production and sales as expected and forced to reduce its prices to match the landed price of imports.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Lyfius Pharma’s 15,000 tonnes Pen G facility in Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh in October 2024. Aurobindo Pharma had said the facility represented a strategic ₹2,500 crore investment under the Centre’s PLI scheme for pharmaceutical sector.
India manufactured Penicillin G until the late 1980s. However, following globalisation, imports led to closure of all plants producing the antibiotic in the country. In March 2024, then Union Minister for Chemicals and Fertilisers and Health and Family Welfare Mansukh Mandaviya said the government was working on bringing back production of Penicillin G in India after three decades.
Earlier this year, Aurobindo Pharma said it expected to produce more than 10,000 metric tonnes on annualised basis over the following 12 months.
